Synod of Alençon
sin'əd əv ah-lahn-sōn'
n. (the national synod of the French Reformed churches at Alençon in 1637, which examined and acquitted Moise Amyraut)
Greek sunodos, a meeting; Alençon, a town in Normandy.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Synod of Alençon was the twenty-sixth national synod of the Reformed churches of France, meeting in 1637. Its most consequential business was the case of Moise Amyraut and Paul Testard, professors at the Academy of Saumur, whose writings, especially Amyraut's Brief Treatise on Predestination of 1634, had been charged with error. Amyraut taught a hypothetical universalism: that God decreed first to save all men through Christ on condition of faith, and then, since no man would believe of himself, decreed to give faith to the elect; so that Christ died for all sufficiently and conditionally, and for the elect effectually. Pierre du Moulin and others accused him of overturning the Canons of Dort. At Alençon, Amyraut and Testard explained themselves, affirming that faith is the gift of God to the elect alone and that the condition of the universal decree is one no man can fulfil without grace. The synod accepted their explanations and acquitted them, while forbidding them to use certain expressions and enjoining silence on the controversy. The silence was not kept, the debate continued for decades, and the Helvetic Consensus of 1675 was framed in part against Saumur. The Canons of Dort had said plainly what Christ said: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and acquittal as a judicial discharge from an accusation.

expand to see more

SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council, either provincial or general.

ACQUIT'TAL, n. A judicial setting free or deliverance from the charge of an offense.

HYPOTHET'ICAL, a. Including a supposition; conditional; assumed without proof.

Joh 17:9 — "I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine."

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

Modern Corruption

A French synod that acquitted Amyraut's hypothetical universalism with a warning.

expand to see more

The dictionary names Amyraut's scheme of a universal conditional decree as a departure from the Reformed doctrine of particular redemption, however orthodox his explanations at Alençon. A decree to save all on a condition God has decreed not to supply to all does not describe the Christ who prays “not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9), or the church He “hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

The synod's decision is a lesson in what acquittal with a warning accomplishes. It kept the peace for a season and left the question open for the next generation, which spent its strength on it while the crown prepared the Revocation. The principle to recover is that synods should decide doctrinal questions plainly, as Dort did, rather than enjoin a silence no one keeps.

Usage

"“I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15) — the doctrine at issue."

"“I pray not for the world” (Joh 17:9) — a particular intercession."

"“purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — a definite redemption."
